claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its subsets are primarily governed by atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Atomic-scale lattice distortion modulates dislocation pinning.
Reducing the constituent count from five elements to four or three decreases lattice distortion.
Reduced lattice distortion makes dislocation pinning less effective.
Less effective dislocation pinning lowers yield strength and alters failure mechanisms.
Atomic-size variation and chemical-bonding differences produce local lattice distortion and heterogeneous dislocation-pinning sites.
The quinary alloy has greater lattice distortion than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater lattice distortion in the quinary alloy increases dislocation pinning and raises yield strength.
Reduced lattice distortion in quaternary and ternary alloys facilitates dislocation motion.
Quaternary and ternary subsets should have lower yield strength than equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Quaternary and ternary subsets should exhibit altered strain-hardening rates that correlate with reduced lattice distortion.
Lower-constituent-count alloys should exhibit narrower distributions of lattice parameters.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline exhibits high yield strength and distinct dislocation-pinning behavior because of pronounced lattice distortion.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to single-phase FCC alloys tested at room temperature and moderate strain rates.
Secondary phases, extreme loading, or significant chemical ordering may invalidate the proposed relationship.
The magnitude of strength reduction and deformation changes depends on which elements are removed and on their contributions to lattice distortion.
